summary: The mawlid (celebration of the Prophet's birthday) is considered bid'ah by the majority of classical and Athari scholars. Some classical scholars permitted certain modest forms of observance with specific conditions. This article presents both positions accurately.
content:
The mawlid al-Nabi refers to the observance of the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) birth, typically on the 12th of Rabi' al-Awwal (though scholars disagreed even on the date of his birth). The question of its permissibility is a well-known intra-Sunni scholarly discussion.

**Primary position:** The majority of Athari scholars, and a significant body of classical scholarship, consider the mawlid as formally celebrated — as a religious holiday with gatherings, specific recitations, and festivity — to be bid'ah without basis in the Quran, Sunnah, or the practice of the Companions and the Salaf. This is the position we present first, as it reflects the methodology of the Salaf and the majority of Hanbali scholars.

## The Athari Position: Bid'ah

The strongest argument against mawlid rests on five points:

**1. The Companions did not do it.** The Sahaba loved the Prophet (peace be upon him) more than anyone — more than their own lives. If celebrating his birthday were a means of expressing that love and drawing closer to Allah, they would have done it. They did not. This silence (tark) of the Companions is itself significant.

**2. The practice originated late.** The mawlid as a formal celebration appears historically in the 4th–5th century AH (10th–11th century CE), long after the Salaf. The first well-documented large-scale mawlid was organised by the Fatimid (Ismaili Shia) rulers of Egypt — itself a problematic origin for a practice entering Sunni practice.

**3. The religion was completed.** Allah declared: 'This day I have perfected for you your religion' (5:3). Adding a new annual observance to the calendar of religious practice implies something was missing from the Sunnah — which contradicts this declaration.

**4. Good intentions do not validate innovation.** The 'Abd ibn Mas'ud example (see Bid'ah article) illustrates that sincerity of intention does not validate a religious practice that lacks Prophetic foundation.

**5. Leading Athari scholars' statements:** Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728 AH) wrote against the mawlid. His student Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 751 AH) similarly considered it an innovation. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal's methodology — that acts of worship require a specific textual proof — yields the same conclusion.

## The Permissive Position: Classical Scholars Who Mentioned It

Some classical scholars, writing after the mawlid had become widespread, discussed it and acknowledged certain permissible elements — while imposing conditions. These scholars include:

**Imam Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH)** — in 'Husn al-Maqsad fi Amal al-Mawlid' he defended spending the occasion in acts of remembrance, reciting poetry in praise of the Prophet, and feeding people. His key argument: the Prophet (peace be upon him) fasted on Mondays because he was born on that day (Muslim 1162). Al-Suyuti considered the underlying act (gratitude for the Prophet's birth) as having a textual basis.

**Imam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 852 AH)** — referenced approvingly by later mawlid scholars, though his full position is sometimes overstated. He acknowledged fasting on the day of the Prophet's birth as a basis for gratitude.

**Conditions these scholars attached:**
- Free from anything haram (music, mixing of men and women, exaggeration in praise)
- Limited to acts with independent Sunnah basis (sadaqah, salawat, recitation of Seerah)
- Not treated as a formal religious obligation or sunnah muakkadah
- Not accompanied by beliefs that would elevate the Prophet's status beyond his proper station

**Editorial note:** The Athari evaluation of these scholars' positions is that they were working within a context where the practice had already spread, and were attempting to constrain rather than endorse it fully. Their conditions, if applied strictly, leave very little of what modern mawlid celebrations typically contain.

## What Is Always Encouraged

What is beyond dispute — and endorsed by scholars of all positions — is:

- Increasing salawat (prayers) upon the Prophet (peace be upon him) throughout the year
- Studying the Seerah (biography of the Prophet) and reflecting on his character
- Loving the Prophet (peace be upon him) as Allah commanded: 'The Prophet has more right over the believers than they have over themselves' (33:6)
- Reviving his Sunnah in daily life

These acts need no calendar occasion — they are the continuous practice of a Muslim who loves the Prophet (peace be upon him).

## Summary of Positions

| Position | Scholars | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Bid'ah (not permitted) | Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Baz (d. 1420 AH, modern), majority Hanbali tradition | No Prophetic or Companion basis; religion complete |
| Permitted with conditions | al-Suyuti, some later scholars | Gratitude for the Prophet's birth has Sunnah basis; permissible if free from haram |

Both positions are among legitimate classical scholarly views within Ahl us-Sunnah. Neither scholars who observe modest forms of mawlid within the conditions nor those who avoid it entirely are outside the fold of Ahl us-Sunnah.
evidence_quran: Surah al-Ma'idah 5:3 — 'This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you' (cited against adding new religious observances)
Surah al-Ahzab 33:6 — 'The Prophet has more right over the believers than they have over themselves' (basis for love of the Prophet)
Surah al-Ahzab 33:56 — 'Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, ask Allah to send blessings upon him' (salawat is established independently)
evidence_hadith: Abu Dawud 4607 (sahih) — 'Every bid'ah is going astray' (cited against mawlid as formal observance)
Muslim 1162 — The Prophet fasted on Monday because he was born that day (al-Suyuti cited this as a basis for gratitude-based observance)
Bukhari 2697, Muslim 1718 — 'Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected'
scholar_positions: **Against (bid'ah):** Ibn Taymiyyah (Iqtida al-Sirat al-Mustaqim), Ibn al-Qayyim, the Hanbali tradition, and many modern scholars including Ibn Baz (d. 1420 AH). **Permissive with conditions:** al-Suyuti (Husn al-Maqsad), Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (cited approvingly in later scholarship), some later Shafi'i and Maliki scholars. Both positions are within Ahl us-Sunnah. The Athari/primary position on this platform is that formal celebration is bid'ah; increasing salawat and studying Seerah year-round is the Prophetically established alternative.
